narrative:
The model estimates a 44% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

Three main factors shaped this outlook. First, your total years of experience across all jobs stands out as the strongest influence, pulling the prediction toward staying. With only 1-5 years overall, you fall into the most common group among employees the model expects to remain, yet the pattern shows that limited cumulative experience often signals higher future mobility in this dataset.

Second, having received other job offers while working here was the next biggest driver and pushed the prediction toward leaving. This factor indicates that external opportunities can make departure more likely, even when other conditions look stable.

Third, your high emotional commitment to the organization worked in your favor, pulling the prediction back toward staying. Employees who feel this level of psychological attachment are generally more likely to remain.

Taken together, your solid emotional ties and moderate experience level are encouraging, but the presence of outside offers created enough concern to tip the overall risk above the promotion threshold.

The organization should discuss retention measures with you, such as clearer career paths or addressing any unmet needs signaled by those external opportunities. You may also want to reflect on what those offers offered that might be missing here.
